analysis.one_liner: Strips EPA funding to enforce any cap-and-trade program or new greenhouse gas limits on power plants and factories.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with less than a month left in the 111th Congress, was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Environmental Protection Agency from spending any money to run a cap-and-trade program for greenhouse gases or to enforce any new requirement limiting greenhouse gas emissions from power plants and factories issued or taking effect after January 1, 2011 [S2][S3]. That would cover Clean Air Act standards and permitting rules for stationary sources like coal plants and industrial facilities [S3]. It was introduced on December 9, 2010, weeks before the 111th Congress ended, and never advanced [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal-fired power plants and other large stationary sources of greenhouse gas emissions, who would avoid carbon limits, allowance costs, and permitting requirements. Energy-intensive industries would also avoid compliance costs that could be passed through electricity and goods prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal plants and large industrial emitters

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal funds from being used by the EPA to implement or enforce a cap-and-trade program, defined as any program distributing limited emission allowances for greenhouse gases [S2][S3].

Blocks funding for any new statutory or regulatory requirement on greenhouse gas emissions from stationary sources taking effect after January 1, 2011, including Clean Air Act standards and permitting rules for power plants and industrial facilities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear increased air pollution and the unchecked costs of climate change. The EPA would lose its funding-based ability to carry out greenhouse gas rules for power plants and factories.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via pollution and climate costs

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave greenhouse gas emissions from power plants and industrial facilities without new federal limits, transferring the full cost of those emissions to the public in the form of pollution and climate damage [S2][S3].
Rather than rewriting environmental law, the bill would use the appropriations process to defund enforcement, leaving a gap in which existing mandates could not be carried out [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection supporters would raise in reverse: EPA greenhouse gas permitting and standards do impose real compliance costs on utilities and energy-intensive manufacturers, costs that can show up in electricity prices and plant closures — which is the burden this bill sought to lift [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a concrete, concentrated benefit — relief from carbon rules and cap-and-trade costs for large emitters — while distributing the costs broadly and diffusely across the public as pollution and long-term climate risk. It offered no replacement policy for limiting those emissions. On balance the benefits flow to a narrow set of emitters and the costs to everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the 111th Congress and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up before Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Poe (R-TX) introduced the bill on December 9, 2010, with 26 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].
Because no cap-and-trade bill had been enacted and the restriction applied only to future EPA action, the bill's death meant EPA retained the authority and funding it already had [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA kept its existing authority and funding to regulate greenhouse gases from power plants and factories, and the public kept the pollution limits the bill would have defunded. The coal-fired utilities and large emitters the bill would have shielded gained nothing, since EPA rules remained in place and the incoming Congress's separate efforts played out elsewhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA and people protected by its rules

for.name: Rep. Ted Poe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to defund EPA enforcement of cap-and-trade and new greenhouse gas rules for stationary sources.

for.name: 26 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from the House Republican minority.

against.name: Chairman Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee; the committee scheduled no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, in a chamber where Democrats held 253 of 431 seats; the bill received no Democratic support and no committee action.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plants and other large industrial emitters
industries.note: The bill would lift Clean Air Act standards, permitting requirements, and any cap-and-trade costs off stationary sources of greenhouse gases [S3]. The industry's savings come directly from rules the public relies on to limit pollution and climate damage [S2][S3].
Blocking cap-and-trade removes the carbon-pricing demand that drives investment in low-emission generation [S2][S3].
